summary: I followed README.md and docs/getting-started.md literally inside the container, in $TMPDIR/adopt-firsthour: a four-file JS app, then init, the first check, a payments node plus an audit aspect, a second node, commit, and a simulated CI clone. The keyless start works well. `yg init` with no TTY lands keyless and says what works. The first check is green and explains why. Deterministic refusals, relation-undeclared-dependency and type-without-when-with-mapping all give a concrete, pasteable fix. The first hour breaks in four places: (1) the flagship example is a judgment rule, so a keyless adopter can never get it green, and `Next:` sends them into an `--approve` that aborts; (2) the agent manual (`yg prime`) in 6.1.0 still describes the removed `yg verdict record` as a lock writer; (3) three things the docs promise are not what the CLI does: that CI is unaffected by auto_approve, that a node's type must exist and declare `when:`, and that aspect-less nodes are free and green; (4) "pair" and "lock" are never defined on the first-hour path, and the report labels non-pair structural errors as "N pairs". After an hour the adopter understands nodes, aspects and approve roughly correctly. Three things they get wrong: that types matter from day one (they do not, until a first type appears and every existing node goes red at once), what a pair is, and whether CI runs their check code.

CHANGELOG [Unreleased] line 16 and docs/the-lock.md:122 say the channel is gone.
surviving.adopter_impact: The agent's standing manual tells it there is a second way to write verdicts that skips the configured reviewer. An agent stuck with no reviewer (the keyless path) will try that sanctioned-looking route and hit an unknown command. It also learns a lock model that contradicts the 6.1.0 one-judge rule.
surviving.suggested_fix: Remove `yg verdict record` from rules.ts line 20, so the lock writers are `--approve`, `log merge-resolve` and the upgrade migration. Delete the parenthetical in the `--approve` table row. Drop "verdict" from the cli-reference topic's description. Add a test that fails when prime output names a command that does not exist.
surviving.verifier: Checked on release/6.1.0 at 007473ad. source/cli/src/templates/rules.ts:20 still lists `yg verdict record` as a lock writer, and the `yg check --approve` table row does too ("The one other writer of verdicts is `yg verdict record`..."). surviving.title: The keyless start's flagship example is a judgment rule; `Next:` then points at an `--approve` that aborts
surviving.where: README.md:52-56; docs/getting-started.md:124-177; `yg check` suggestedNext
surviving.evidence: After a keyless `yg init` (the default with no TTY), I followed getting-started step 3 exactly: aspect with content.md, node mapping src/payments/. `yg check` → Errors (2): unverified + "config-reviewer-missing  A judgment rule has no judge", yet "Next: yg check --approve  (fills 1 unverified; 1 error remain — need code/graph fixes)". Following Next: `yg check --approve` → "aborted — 1 problem must be fixed before anything runs ... A judgment rule has no judge" EXIT=1. The config-reviewer-missing fix says "Run yg init and pick 'Configure reviewer'". With no TTY, `yg init` answers ".yggdrasil/ already exists and no reconfiguration flag was given (no TTY to open the menu)", so it takes a second hop to reach `--provider`. README:56: "`yg check --approve` verifies it."
surviving.adopter_impact: The README and getting-started sell "None for now" as a real answer, then hand over an audit rule that only an LLM can judge. The adopter, or their agent obeying "Follow it" for suggestedNext, runs the suggested command and gets an abort. The "need code/graph fixes" hint points them at the wrong fix: the missing reviewer is a config problem.
surviving.suggested_fix: When config-reviewer-missing is present, make it suggestedNext and put the literal command `yg init --provider <name> [--model <m>]` in its fix. In getting-started step 3, either make the first example a check.mjs rule or add a line: if you chose None for now, run `yg init --provider claude-code` before `--approve`. Classify the remaining-error hint by kind instead of always saying "code/graph".
surviving.verifier: Reproduced after a keyless init: a content.md aspect on the payments node gives Errors(2) with unverified plus config-reviewer-missing, then "Next: yg check --approve  (fills 1 unverified; 1 error remain — need code/graph fixes)". Running that aborts with EXIT=1 ("A judgment rule has no judge"). A non-TTY `yg init` then prints "Pass one: --provider <name> [--model <m>]". So the wrong Next line and the "code/graph" misclassification are real. I downgraded it for three reasons. getting-started.md:65-72 says to add a judge "whenever you write your first judgment rule" and gives `yg init --provider claude-code`. The keyless init output says "Add a judge for judgment rules any time: yg init --provider <name>". The abort message names the fix, so recovery takes one or two clear hops. Only the README path skips the bridge. One wasted command is friction, not a blocker.

surviving.title: The CI recipe uses a bare `yg check` while the docs promise CI scripts use explicit flags; auto_approve fills in CI
surviving.where: README.md:152-153; docs/getting-started.md:289-292 vs docs/getting-started.md:309-313 and docs/how-it-works.md:41-44

surviving.suggested_fix: Change the gate line in README and getting-started to `yg check --no-approve`, matching how-it-works. Alternatively, make check refuse config-driven fills when `CI` is set.
surviving.verifier: README.md ("- run: npx @chrisdudek/yg check") and getting-started.md:291-292 both use a bare `yg check` as the gate. getting-started.md:312-313 says "CI scripts always use explicit flags and are unaffected". how-it-works.md:40-44 uses `--no-approve` and says the CI recipe spells the flags out, and configuration.md's CI note says the same. check.ts falls back to config.auto_approve and has no CI detection (git grep for process.env.CI and GITHUB_ACTIONS finds nothing). Live run with auto_approve: full and CI=true, bare `yg check`: "auto-approve: full — bare 'yg check' will call the reviewer." followed by "yg check --approve aborted". yg-config.yaml is committed, so a "local convenience" setting reaches CI.

surviving.title: With the architecture init writes (`node_types: {}`), any node type string is silently accepted, contradicting getting-started, and it turns red later
surviving.where: source/cli/src/core/checks/architecture.ts:316-320 (early return when node_types is empty); docs/getting-started.md:142-147
surviving.evidence: getting-started:142: "A node's type must declare `when:` before the node can carry a mapping at all". Live in a fresh init: node with `type: totally-made-up`, mapping src/a/ → "yg check: PASS (1 warning)  1 nodes · 1/5 files (1 node-owned...)", and `yg context --node a` → "a — d (totally-made-up)". After adding one unrelated type `service` with `when:` → "FAIL ... type-undefined  1 pairs  1 nodes  Allowed types: service. ... Node type 'totally-made-up' is not defined". In the main scratch project the payments node had `type: module` with no such type defined, and it went green through approve.
surviving.adopter_impact: The adopter, or their agent, learns that types are free-form labels and maps several nodes that way. The first architecture type anyone adds, even one unrelated to those nodes, turns every existing node red at once. The rule the docs teach is not the rule the tool enforces.
surviving.suggested_fix: Run checkNodeTypesExist and type-without-when-with-mapping even when node_types is empty (a fresh init has nothing to be lenient toward). If leniency is intended, add a warning such as "node type 'x' is not defined; it will be required once yg-architecture.yaml declares any type", and correct getting-started:142.
surviving.verifier: Confirmed in the source and live. architecture.ts:318-320 returns early when node_types is empty, so checkNodeTypesExist never runs. A payments node with `type: module` and no types defined gives no type-undefined error. After I added an unrelated `service` type with `when:`, check reports "type-undefined 1 pairs 1 nodes ... Node type 'module' is not defined" with a concrete fix. This contradicts getting-started.md:142. I downgraded it because the getting-started flow has the agent define the type with `when:`, so an adopter following the docs never hits the lenient path. The deferred error is also explicit and says exactly what to add.

surviving.title: Brownfield guidance says aspect-less nodes are "cheap" and CI stays green, but mapping them turns on blocking relation conformance
surviving.where: docs/getting-started.md:248-270
surviving.evidence: getting-started:256-258: "Nodes without aspects are cheap — just a `yg-node.yaml` with a directory mapping. They produce no pairs, so there is nothing to verify and nothing to record. They count as covered for free." Step 4: "`yg check` passes — CI is green". Live: I added an aspect-less node `users` (mapping src/users/, whose file imports ../payments/charge.js) → "yg check: FAIL ... relation-undeclared-dependency  1 pairs  1 nodes ... Declare the missing relation(s) in .yggdrasil/model/users/yg-node.yaml ... - users  src/users/users.js:1 → payments". While the file was only type-covered, the same import was silent.
surviving.adopter_impact: On a 200-file repo, following steps 1-4 ("5-8 nodes without aspects for broad directory mappings") makes CI go red on every cross-node import, which a real codebase will have. The adopter expected an instant green baseline and instead gets a wall of blocking errors the page never mentioned.
surviving.suggested_fix: In the brownfield section, say that every mapped node is checked live for undeclared dependencies on other mapped nodes, that the fix is a `relations:` entry (the error prints the stanza), and that relations must stay acyclic. Add "declare relations" as an explicit step between creating nodes and expecting green, or point to progressive mode for inherited debt.
surviving.verifier: I added an aspect-less node `users` mapping src/users/, which imports ../payments/charge.js. Result: FAIL, with "relation-undeclared-dependency 1 pairs 1 nodes" in Errors. It even says "no relation type is allowed from module to module; either change a node's type or update the allowed relations in yg-architecture.yaml". So the fix can require an architecture change as well as a relations entry. getting-started.md:256-269 says these nodes are "cheap ... nothing to verify" and that after step 4 "`yg check` passes — CI is green", with no mention of relations. docs/nodes.md:90 does mention the built-in relation check in a parenthetical. The brownfield section a 200-file adopter follows does not, so the promised green baseline fails on almost any real codebase.

surviving.title: The knowledge topic claims "CI executes no adopter code" while the documented CI recipe runs every check.mjs
surviving.where: source/cli/src/templates/knowledge/writing-deterministic-aspects.ts:33-34 vs README.md:152, docs/getting-started.md:289-290
surviving.evidence: `yg knowledge read writing-deterministic-aspects`: "**Plain `yg check` never executes a deterministic check** — it validates the entry by hashing ... So CI executes no adopter code; check's cost is hashing only." The recommended CI recipe's first step is `yg check --approve --only-deterministic`, which runs check.mjs. Live in a fresh clone: "Filling 1 unverified pairs across 1 nodes — 1 deterministic (no cost)... 1/1 filled (1 ok)". The `yg pack` help says "Installing a package runs its author's code on every check".
surviving.adopter_impact: Someone deciding whether to install a third-party rule package, or to run CI on untrusted PRs, is told CI runs none of their check code. In fact the recommended pipeline runs every check.mjs, packaged ones included, on each CI run. That is a wrong trust model.
surviving.suggested_fix: Reword to: "Plain `yg check` never executes a check; the CI recipe's cache-rebuild step (`--approve --only-deterministic`) does run every check.mjs, including installed packages, because the deterministic cache is gitignored."
surviving.verifier: writing-deterministic-aspects.ts:33-35 reads: "Plain `yg check` never executes a deterministic check ... So CI executes no adopter code; check's cost is hashing only." The documented CI recipe's first step (README, getting-started.md:289-290) is `yg check --approve --only-deterministic`. Live, it printed "[det] requires-audit on node:payments" and "1/1 filled", which means it executed check.mjs. The claim about the first half is true of plain check, but the conclusion about CI is false for the recommended pipeline. That is a wrong trust statement in the agent's knowledge base, and the agent may repeat it to a user deciding whether to run CI on untrusted PRs or install packages.

surviving.title: "Pair" (and the lock) are never defined on the first-hour path, and non-pair structural errors are reported as "N pairs"
surviving.where: README.md, docs/how-it-works.md, docs/getting-started.md (no definition; first defined in docs/the-lock.md:29-38); `yg check` grouped header
surviving.evidence: README.md and how-it-works.md contain no "pair"; getting-started first uses it in sample output line 158 ("unverified (not yet reviewed)  1 pairs  1 nodes") and in "They produce no pairs" (257), and its "Core" list (304-315) defines Node, Aspect, check and approve but not pair or lock. The prime says the relation check "is NOT an aspect", yet live output reads "relation-undeclared-dependency  1 pairs  1 nodes", "type-without-when-with-mapping  1 pairs  1 nodes" and "type-undefined  1 pairs  1 nodes".
surviving.adopter_impact: The adopter cannot work out what the count in every error header means, what `--approve` fills, or why "no pairs" should mean "free". The CLI then applies the word to structural and relation errors that are not (aspect, unit) pairs, so the mental model it implies is wrong.
surviving.suggested_fix: Add pair (one aspect × one unit, the unit of cost and caching) and lock (the hashed verdict record) to getting-started's "Core" list, linking /the-lock. In the grouped renderer, use "N nodes" or "N issues" for non-pair codes and keep "pairs" for verdict groups.
surviving.verifier: README.md and how-it-works.md contain no "pair". getting-started uses it only in sample output and in "They produce no pairs", and its Core list (304-315) never defines it. the-lock.md:29-38 defines it and admits the concept pages "deliberately leave it out". The mislabel reproduces live on non-pair codes: "yaml-invalid 1 pairs 1 nodes", "orphaned-aspect 1 pairs 1 nodes", "type-undefined 1 pairs 1 nodes", "relation-undeclared-dependency 1 pairs 1 nodes". The lock is at least introduced in how-it-works (step 3). I downgraded it because "N pairs" reads naturally as an item count, and no adopter gets stuck or acts wrongly because of it. It is real jargon friction.

surviving.title: On a fresh clone, cached deterministic verdicts show as "unverified (not yet reviewed)" with no hint that a free cache rebuild is the fix
surviving.where: `yg check` in a fresh clone; unverified group message
surviving.evidence: Committed a green project, cloned it, then `yg check` → "FAIL ... unverified (not yet reviewed)  1 pairs  1 nodes  The lock holds no entry for this pair, or its inputs changed since the verdict was recorded (source edit, aspect edit, or a fill that did not complete) ... Fix: yg check --approve". No mention of the gitignored `.yg-lock.deterministic.json`.
surviving.adopter_impact: A teammate who pulls a green main sees the rule reported as never reviewed and suspects the author skipped verification. The suggested fix is a general `--approve` rather than the free, keyless `--approve --only-deterministic`.
surviving.suggested_fix: When the missing entry belongs to a deterministic pair and the local cache file is absent or empty, say "local deterministic cache not built on this checkout" and suggest `yg check --approve --only-deterministic`.
surviving.verifier: I committed a green project with a deterministic check.mjs and cloned it. Plain `yg check` in the clone reports "unverified (not yet reviewed) 1 pairs" with "Fix: yg check --approve", and says nothing about the gitignored `.yg-lock.deterministic.json`, which I confirmed is listed in .yggdrasil/.gitignore. The suggested `--approve` does work, since deterministic fills are free and committed LLM verdicts stay valid, and getting-started's CI section and the-lock.md explain the cache. So minor is right: the wording ("not yet reviewed") misattributes the cause, but it does not block anyone.

surviving.title: The approve summary says "all expected pairs hold valid verdicts" immediately before a FAIL with a refusal
surviving.where: `yg check --approve` stderr summary
surviving.evidence:
"  [det] requires-audit on node:payments — refused
... 1/1 filled (0 ok, 1 refused)
0 reviewer calls made — all expected pairs hold valid verdicts
yg check: FAIL ... enforced  1 pairs  1 nodes  aspect 'requires-audit' ... src/payments/charge.js:3: payment mutation without audit()"
surviving.adopter_impact: "Valid verdicts" reads as "everything passed" right above a blocking refusal. The adopter cannot tell whether the run succeeded. "Valid" (hash-current) and "passing" are different, and neither term has been defined for them yet.
surviving.suggested_fix: Say "every expected pair now has a current verdict (N approved, M refused)", or omit the line when any refusal was recorded.
surviving.verifier: Reproduced exactly with a refusing check.mjs: "[det] requires-audit on node:payments — refused", "1/1 filled (0 ok, 1 refused)", "0 reviewer calls made — all expected pairs hold valid verdicts", then "yg check: FAIL ... enforced 1 pairs". The same summary line appears even when a yaml-invalid error blocks everything and 0 pairs were filled. The FAIL header and the refusal block right after it make the outcome recoverable, so minor.

surviving.title: A fresh init lists Yggdrasil's own files as uncovered to-dos, and every hint says to map or move them
surviving.where: `yg check` after `yg init`; `yg type-suggest`; docs/getting-started.md:225-231
surviving.evidence: The first check on a fresh init lists "uncovered (10)  .clinerules/yggdrasil.md  .gitattributes  AGENTS.md  CLAUDE.md ..." with "Fix: Map these files to a node...". `yg type-suggest --file AGENTS.md` → "1. Move file under a path matching an existing type's when  2. Refactor file to satisfy a type's content predicate  3. Add a new type". `yg init --upgrade` → "Agent rules already up to date — nothing changed." (no exclusion stanza). getting-started:225-231 presents these files as a problem only for older projects, and README:50 calls the list "your to-do".
surviving.adopter_impact: Nearly half the first to-do list is files the tool itself wrote, and the only guidance is to map, move or refactor them. Nothing suggests `coverage.excluded`.
surviving.suggested_fix: Have fresh `yg init` write the files it creates into `coverage.excluded`, or have the uncovered hint and type-suggest recognise Yggdrasil-managed files and suggest excluding them.
surviving.verifier: In a fresh keyless init, the first `yg check` lists uncovered (6), and 4 of those are Yggdrasil's own files (.clinerules/yggdrasil.md, .gitattributes, AGENTS.md, CLAUDE.md). The hint is "Map these files to a node... Your architecture has no type for this file yet." `yg type-suggest --file AGENTS.md` suggests moving or refactoring the file or adding a type. `yg init --upgrade` prints "Agent rules already up to date — nothing changed." with no exclusion stanza. The exclusion advice at getting-started.md:225-231 sits inside the "Whole-repo default" box for older projects only. They are non-blocking in require-nothing mode, so minor.

summary: I tested the daily loop and the gate in a scratch project in the dev container ($TMPDIR/adopt-gate: `init --no-reviewer`, two nodes, a check.mjs rule, a content.md rule, a log_required type; then an unreachable ollama reviewer, auto_approve set to deterministic and to full, and a fresh clone). The deterministic path reads well. Each message gives a what, a why and a fix. The log gate names the node and the exact `yg log add` command. `--only-deterministic` says plainly which LLM pairs it skipped. `auto_approve: full` announces itself. The weak spots all sit where the report hands the adopter a next step. On a keyless project with one prose rule, the documented free CI gate (`--approve --only-deterministic`) refuses to run at all. An advisory prose rule blocks the build, although the docs say advisory never blocks. When the reviewer is unreachable, stdout and `--json` still say "Next: yg check --approve", and only stderr says that re-running will not help, so an agent loops. The published CI recipe uses a bare `yg check`, which `auto_approve` can quietly turn into a paid reviewer call. The agent rules that `yg prime` prints still name the removed `yg verdict record` as a way to write verdicts. The report also uses one word, "unverified (not yet reviewed)", for three different situations: never judged, stale, and a cache miss on a fresh clone. That gives adopters the wrong idea of what the next command will cost.

surviving.title: On a keyless project, the 'free, keyless CI gate' (--approve --only-deterministic) refuses to run once one prose rule exists; the retry hint drops the flag and suggestedNext points at a command that also refuses
surviving.where: yg check --approve --only-deterministic (and yg check suggestedNext) on a project from `yg init --no-reviewer` with one content.md aspect; docs/cli-reference.md:566, :628; source/cli/src/templates/rules.ts:94
surviving.evidence:
`yg check --approve --only-deterministic` →
"yg check --approve aborted — 1 problem must be fixed before anything runs. ... nothing ran and nothing was written.
Fix the errors below, then re-run: yg check --approve
A judgment rule has no judge: yg-config.yaml has no reviewer: section." [exit 1]. The deterministic no-q pair stays unverified. The plain `yg check` printed just before it ends with "Next: yg check --approve  (fills 2 unverified; 1 error remain — need code/graph fixes)", and that command aborts the same way. The docs promise otherwise: cli-reference:566 "infrastructure failures (provider unreachable, no reviewer configured, ...) write nothing and leave the pair unverified" (per pair, not a whole-run abort), and the agent rules (rules.ts:94) say "`--only-deterministic` is the free, keyless CI gate (no reviewer at all)". getting-started:52 says script rules and the CI gate "all work immediately, for free".
surviving.adopter_impact: A keyless adopter who writes their first judgment rule finds that CI step 1, the documented free cache rebuild, fails, and no script rule can be verified anywhere. The retry line tells them to run `yg check --approve`, which fails in the same way. An agent that follows suggestedNext is stuck in a loop.
surviving.suggested_fix: Let `--only-deterministic` skip the config-reviewer-missing structural abort, since it never calls a reviewer. Report the missing judge as a finding on the LLM pairs only. Make the retry line repeat the flags the user actually ran. Rank config-reviewer-missing above `unverified` in suggestedNext, so Next never names a command that is certain to abort.
surviving.verifier: Reproduced in $TMPDIR/verify-daily-loop (yg init --no-reviewer, check.mjs aspect no-q on api, content.md aspect explain on db, then a handler.ts edit). `yg check --approve --only-deterministic` printed "yg check --approve aborted — 1 problem must be fixed before anything runs ... nothing ran and nothing was written. Fix the errors below, then re-run: yg check --approve / A judgment rule has no judge" and exited 1, so the det pair was not refreshed. The plain check before it gave "Next: yg check --approve  (fills 1 unverified; 1 error remain ...)", and --json suggestedNext was 'yg check --approve'. This contradicts cli-reference.md:565-567, which lists infra failures including 'no reviewer configured' as per-pair and leaving the pair unverified, and rules.ts:124, which calls --only-deterministic 'the free, keyless CI gate (no reviewer at all)'. With an unreachable reviewer configured, --only-deterministic runs fine, so only the case with no reviewer section aborts. Downgraded from blocker: the abort message itself names the way out (configure a reviewer). getting-started also tells keyless adopters to 'Add a judge ... whenever you write your first judgment rule'. The build is red in this state anyway, because the prose pair cannot be judged. The real cost is that script-rule results cannot be refreshed and the retry and Next lines point at a command that is certain to abort. That is serious confusion, but the adopter is not permanently stuck.

surviving.title: An advisory prose rule turns the build red when no reviewer is configured, contradicting 'advisory never blocks'
surviving.where: yg check with a content.md aspect set to `status: advisory` and no reviewer: section; docs/aspect-status.md:41, docs/getting-started.md:203-205
surviving.evidence: With explain at `status: advisory`, `yg check` prints "Errors (1): config-reviewer-missing  A judgment rule has no judge ...". The advisory pair itself is listed under Warnings as "unverified (not yet reviewed)". [exit 1]. The docs say: aspect-status.md:41 "advisory never blocks (whether a pair is refused or merely unverified)", and its only listed exception is prompt-too-large. getting-started tip: "Authoring it as `status: advisory` runs the reviewer and lists refusals as warnings, without blocking CI."
surviving.adopter_impact: An adopter follows the 'start new aspects at advisory' advice precisely to keep CI green while trying out a first judgment rule, and CI goes red anyway. The docs say this cannot happen, so the adopter concludes the status system is broken, or flips the rule to draft, which stops it running at all.
surviving.suggested_fix: Choose one behaviour and document it. Either make config-reviewer-missing follow the strictest status among the affected pairs (a warning when all are advisory), or add it to the list of status-independent exceptions in aspect-status.md and the getting-started tip.
surviving.verifier: Reproduced. With explain at `status: advisory` and no reviewer, `yg check` puts config-reviewer-missing under Errors (1), lists the advisory pair under Warnings as 'unverified (not yet reviewed)', and exits 1. aspect-status.md:41 says 'advisory never blocks (whether a pair is refused or merely unverified)', and rules.ts:122 repeats that. So the contradiction in the text is real. Downgraded: the blocking item is a project-config error, not the advisory pair. Its Fix line and Next line both say exactly what to do ('Run yg init and pick Configure reviewer ...'). getting-started's documented order also has the adopter add a judge when they write the first judgment rule. The advisory tip ('runs the reviewer and lists refusals as warnings') assumes a reviewer exists. The adopter is not left guessing.

surviving.title: When the reviewer is unreachable, only stderr says 're-running will not help'; the stdout report and --json both give 'Next: yg check --approve'

summary: An adopter can choose and write a reviewer config from docs/configuration.md alone. The provider table, the per-tier fields, the yg-secrets overlay and the copilot-cli paragraph are accurate, and the config parser gives good guardrails: unknown tier keys, a missing openai-compatible endpoint, and --model required for copilot-cli. Everything after "configured" is where it breaks down. Non-interactive `yg init --provider` writes a reviewer whose binary is missing without a word, which contradicts the CHANGELOG. At `yg check --approve` every failure comes out as one of three generic strings: "unreachable… endpoint did not respond", "Reviewer unavailable" or "Anthropic request failed". That covers a missing binary, a missing key, a bad key, a bad model and a timeout. The real cause (the CLI's stderr, the HTTP status) is dropped, and for the CLI providers it is dropped even with debug: true. The purpose-built copilot "not found, install it or set YG_COPILOT_BIN" message never reaches the user. The runs then close by telling the user to re-run the same command. Two smaller things make it harder to follow. The docs disagree with themselves and with the code on the claude-code default model (haiku vs sonnet), which bears on cost. And `yg prime`, the agent's required first read, still describes the removed `yg verdict record` as a second judge.

surviving.title: CLI reviewer failures (auth, bad model, timeout) all collapse to 'Reviewer unavailable'; stderr is thrown away even with debug: true

summary: The agent layer's outer shell holds up. `yg init` writes one identical digest into AGENTS.md, .clinerules/yggdrasil.md and a CLAUDE.md `@AGENTS.md` import. `yg prime --digest` matches the installed block. surviving.title: With no reviewer, `--approve` (even `--only-deterministic`) aborts the whole run; prime teaches per-pair fail-closed, and the remedy is a wizard an agent cannot use

surviving.evidence: Prime line 79: "Refused (infrastructure — fail closed) → when a pair cannot be verified at all (… NO reviewer is configured for an effective non-draft LLM pair …), `yg check --approve` writes NOTHING for that pair." surviving.adopter_impact: A keyless adopter's agent adds its first prose rule. From then on even the free deterministic fill stops, so script-rule refusals disappear from view. summary: Most single-cause failures are handled well. A default-exported check.mjs, a typo in the architecture file, a missing relation, a lock file with conflict markers, a past review_by date and a mistyped advise id each print what went wrong, why and what to do next. Things break down when one failure causes others, or when a fill fails partway. Examples: a log.md conflict mid-merge, a judgment rule in a project set up without a reviewer, a copilot-cli reviewer whose binary is missing, a fill that crashes or hits a malformed suppression marker. In those cases the CLI points at a command that refuses to run, prints a generic message that hides a specific one it already has, or loops back to `yg check --approve`. The 6.0.0 to 6.1.0 upgrade story is weak. The agent manual `yg prime` still teaches the removed `yg verdict record`, which now fails as an unknown command. The CHANGELOG uses no BREAKING marker, although earlier releases do. It files a required drill-corpus migration under Fixed. It never tells the adopter to run `yg init --upgrade`, and it contradicts itself about `yg-review/1`.

surviving.title: Mid-merge log conflict: the Fix command refuses to run, and the step actually needed is one the messages forbid
surviving.where: `yg check` log-conflict issue → `yg log merge-resolve --node <n>`; docs/the-lock.md:114; docs/cli-reference.md:718-722
surviving.evidence:
Two branches each ran `yg log add --node billing`, then `git merge feat-a` left conflicts in log.md and yg-lock.logs.json.
1) `yg check` → lock-invalid: "take one side wholesale: git checkout --ours ... Then run `yg check --approve`". It says nothing about the conflicted log.md.
2) After that step, `yg check` → "log-conflict ... hand-stitching the two sides breaks the append-only integrity hashes — the merge must be reconciled structurally. Fix: yg log merge-resolve --node billing", yet the report ends "Next: yg check --approve  (fills 1 unverified; 1 error remain)".
3) `yg log merge-resolve --node billing` → "HEAD is not a merge commit ... Run it on the merge commit (git merge --no-ff), or ... name the two sides: --ours <ref> --theirs <ref>" (exit 1). The file still has conflict markers.
It works only if I remove the markers by hand, put both entries in date order, commit the merge, and then run merge-resolve ("Merge-resolve verified ... Log baseline updated."). The docs contradict each other about who does the union. cli-reference: "Validates byte-exact ancestor portion and unions new entries from both branches". the-lock.md: "it reads your merge resolution, it never rewrites it. Never concatenate two log histories by hand."
surviving.adopter_impact: On any team with `log_required` types, parallel branches produce exactly this conflict. The adopter or agent is told not to hand-stitch, is sent to a command that refuses, and is pointed by Next at `--approve`, which cannot clear it. The one working path (hand-merge in date order, commit, then merge-resolve) is written nowhere and is described as forbidden.
surviving.suggested_fix: When log.md contains conflict markers, have the log-conflict message give the real sequence: keep every entry from both sides, remove the markers, order entries by timestamp, commit the merge, then run `yg log merge-resolve --node X`. Better, let merge-resolve read MERGE_HEAD during an in-progress merge and write the union itself. Rank log-conflict above unverified in suggestedNext. Mention conflicted log.md files in the lock-invalid message. Settle whether merge-resolve unions or only verifies, and state it the same way in both docs.
surviving.verifier: Reproduced every step in $TMPDIR/verify-failure-and-upgrade. With a log_required type, two branches each ran `yg log add`, and `git merge feat-a` left UU on log.md and yg-lock.logs.json. (1) lock-invalid tells you to take one side, then `yg check --approve`, and says nothing about the log. (2) Next, check shows log-conflict with the text "hand-stitching the two sides breaks the append-only integrity hashes ... Fix: yg log merge-resolve --node billing", while Next says "yg check --approve (fills 1 unverified; 1 error remain)". (3) merge-resolve fails with "HEAD is not a merge commit" (rc=1). Adding --ours HEAD --theirs feat-a gives "log.md still contains conflict markers ... Resolve all conflicts in log.md, then run yg log merge-resolve again". (4) Hand-union in date order, then commit, then merge-resolve gives "Merge-resolve verified". cli-reference.md:718-724 ("unions new entries ... Never manually concatenate") does contradict the-lock.md:114 ("it reads your merge resolution, it never rewrites it"). I downgraded from blocker for two reasons. The second merge-resolve message does give a next step (resolve the markers). And the-lock.md:114-116 says to run it "from the merge commit" on "your merge resolution", gives the lock→merge-resolve→approve order, and says "put them in date order before running merge-resolve". A careful adopter can reconstruct the path, but the CLI messages loop and the docs wording conflicts.

The code writes only `debugWrite(... omitted ...)`. family-contracts.md says `yg advise` "rejects any `v` it does not name" but does not say it does so silently. With my test file (no evidence block) the text also read "these files cluster tightly (tightness 0)".
surviving.adopter_impact: When Grain moves ahead of the installed yg, which is the usual upgrade skew, its family nominations disappear without a word. The adopter concludes Grain found nothing.
surviving.suggested_fix: Add one Attention line in `yg advise` naming each candidates file skipped and why (unsupported v, unparseable, bad ts), with the next step (upgrade yg or re-run the producer).
surviving.verifier: Confirmed from code rather than by running it. In source/cli/src/cli/advise.ts:155-167, `if (parsed === undefined) continue;` skips an unknown-v file with no output at all, not even debugWrite. A JSON parse error only reaches debugWrite. The function ends with the comment "present-or-omit — absence is silent". docs/family-contracts.md:38 says only "rejects any `v` it does not name" and does not say the rejection is silent. I did not re-verify the 'tightness 0' aside.

surviving.title: The unmapped-file error has a garbled Fix line and unexplained jargon
surviving.where: `yg check` unmapped (file under coverage.required)
surviving.evidence:
"unmapped (1)  lib/q.ts
 Why: Files without graph coverage cannot be modified under the protocol. Your architecture has no type for this file yet.
 Fix: Check ownership candidates: yg context --file <path> yg type-suggest --file <path> can help design one before you decide where it belongs." Also, `yg advise` prints "0 incidents on record — the only external oracle; see .yggdrasil/incidents.md" in a repo where that file does not exist.
surviving.adopter_impact: The Fix line runs two commands together with no separator. "The protocol" is never defined. The adopter cannot tell which command to run or why an unmapped file is 'unmodifiable'.
surviving.suggested_fix: Split into two sentences with clear commands ("Map it to a node (yg context --file <path> lists candidates) or design a type (yg type-suggest --file <path>)"). Replace "under the protocol" with the concrete consequence, which is that it blocks `yg check`.
surviving.verifier: With lib/ under coverage.required and lib/q.ts unmapped, `yg check` prints "Why: Files without graph coverage cannot be modified under the protocol. ... Fix: Check ownership candidates: yg context --file <path> yg type-suggest --file <path> can help design one before you decide where it belongs." The two commands run together with no separator. With no .yggdrasil/incidents.md present (`ls` fails), `yg advise` still prints "0 incidents on record — the only external oracle; see .yggdrasil/incidents.md".
